processing: Medium oxidation with firm shaking, rolled into strips and charcoal roasted, usually medium and sometimes heavier; lighter versions are also described.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May (a mid-season sprouter), as mature shoots with three or four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Stout, slightly broad, dark brown-black strips with a deep roasted, faintly medicinal smell.
appearance_liquor: Deep amber to reddish-brown, clear and dense.
appearance_wet: Thick, dark olive leaves with pronounced red edges, firm and leathery.
taste_profile: Full, dense and savoury: dark roasted grain, a herbal-medicinal depth like dried citrus peel and bitter roots, dark fruit, and a strong, bracing mineral finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, quick pours. A zisha pot suits its heavy roast. It is a tea that rewards patience: the first two steeps are mostly roast, the character arrives from the third.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted over the summer and sold from autumn with the year stated. Because it is usually roasted fairly hard, Tie Luo Han is often better after a year of rest than fresh, and it keeps three to five years or longer sealed and dry; aged lots are sold as chen nian yancha with the year on the label.
description:
Tie Luo Han, the Iron Arhat, is by reputation the oldest of the four famous bushes of Wuyi (si da ming cong, alongside Da Hong Pao, Bai Ji Guan and Shui Jin Gui), and as usually made today it is the heavyweight of the group: dark, dense, savoury and a little medicinal. It is the rock tea to reach for when a Rou Gui feels too bright.

The original bushes are traditionally placed in the Hui Yuan Keng area of the core scenic zone, in the narrow cleft called Gui Dong (ghost cave), though that account is hard to confirm; stories about a Song-dynasty origin and about a monk nicknamed the Iron Arhat are legends, not records, and a Qianlong-era date of around 1782 quoted in the trade is no firmer. The cultivar is now grown in small plots across Wuyi, always in limited quantity.

The leaf is large and thick and is usually given a medium or heavier charcoal roast, though some makers and older descriptions lean lighter and more floral. The roast, combined with the cultivar's own bitterness, is what produces the taste that Chinese drinkers describe as medicinal: think dried tangerine peel, roasted grain, bitter herbs and dark dried fruit, with a long mineral aftertaste that makes the mouth feel cool and clean. There is a folk reputation for it as a remedy for fevers and stomach trouble, which is folklore, but it tells you how the tea tastes.

Brew it hot and quick. The first two steeps are roast-heavy and can seem blunt; by the third the body turns thick, the bitterness folds into sweetness and the herbal depth shows. It lasts eight or more infusions and is excellent cooled down. If a fresh lot tastes harsh, put it away for six months.

When buying, expect to pay famous-bush prices and look for whole, stout strips with a clean roast; genuinely zhengyan Tie Luo Han is scarce, and most of what is sold at modest prices comes from newer plantings outside the core area, which can still be very good. Try it next to Bai Ji Guan, its opposite among the four famous bushes, to see how wide the Wuyi range really is.
sources_note: The Gui Dong / Hui Yuan Keng origin is the standard account; the Song-dynasty dating is legend and is described as such.
history:
Tie Luo Han is one of the four famous bushes of Wuyi and is often called the oldest of them, though firm evidence is thin. The legend behind the name is of a warrior monk with golden-bronze skin, the Iron Arhat. One Wuyi tea seller dates the tea to the Qianlong era, around 1782; that date is the trade's and comes without a record behind it.

Descriptions of the tea also disagree. Some English accounts call it light, with intense green leaf and gentle florals, while modern sellers offer it from medium roast upward. That spread probably says more about makers than about the plant, and the name now covers a fairly wide range of roasts.
